issues.issue: This clause and Section 7(jjj) both warrant that the Mortgagor received all required disclosure materials, the latter adding an executed statement and a file-retention duty. Two overlapping representations on the same subject invite argument about which controls.

The representation turns on 'any circumstances or condition ... that could reasonably be expected to cause investors to regard the Revolving Credit Loan as an unacceptable investment', a standard with no ascertainable boundary and referable to an unidentified body of investors. The clause also repeats the bankruptcy limb twice ('is not in bankruptcy and, the Mortgagor is not insolvent or in bankruptcy').

This clause warrants a monthly-adjusting rate equal to Index plus Gross Margin subject to caps, while Section 1 defines 'Mortgage Rate' as 'the annual rate of interest borne by a Mortgage Note as stated herein' and builds Net Mortgage Rate on it. The rate architecture in the definitions does not fit the adjustable rate warranted here.

'each Revolving Credit Loan requires the payment of a Cancellation Fee, where applicable' is circular: the qualifier 'where applicable' removes whatever content the warranty had. Nothing in the Agreement says when a Cancellation Fee is applicable or what it is.

The clause says each loan matures in either 180 or 300 months and has a Draw Period of 5, 10 or 15 years followed by a ten-year Amortization Period, but a 10-year draw plus 10-year amortization equals 240 months, which is neither permitted term. The two sentences cannot both be true of a 10-year-draw loan.

The list of eligible originators ends with 'or similar institution which is supervised and examined by a federal or state authority', a catch-all whose reach against the enumerated institutions is uncertain. Whether a licensed non-bank mortgage lender qualifies is exactly the ejusdem generis question.

Limb (ix) requires the ground lease term to extend 'at least five years beyond the maturity date', while Section 7(mm) requires a leasehold not to terminate 'less than ten years after the maturity date' of the HELOC. The two leasehold representations set different minimum terms for the same collateral.

Eligibility is measured against 'HELOC Seller's Underwriting Standards', while Section 7(ee) warrants origination in accordance with 'the underwriting guidelines of the related originator' and the recitals show the loans were originated and serviced by others. Which set of standards governs a condominium or PUD loan is unresolved.

'no claims will arise as to broker fees that are double charged' is a warranty about future events by third parties, and 'properly assessed' has no stated benchmark. What breach of this clause looks like, and when, is unclear.

The proviso caps lost note affidavits at 1% 'of the Revolving Credit Loans, in the aggregate', a pool-level test embedded in loan-level representations whose only remedy is loan-by-loan cure, repurchase or substitution under the Section 7 repurchase provision. It is also uncertain how it interacts with Section 4(b)(iii) and the Exhibit 5 schedule of lost notes, which permit affidavits without any stated cap.

This clause warrants that the loan documents 'have been delivered to the Purchaser or its designee', while Section 4(b) requires delivery to the Indenture Trustee or the Custodian and permits a later Mortgage File Delivery Date. The 'except as provided in Section 4(b)' carve-out does not clearly resolve to whom delivery must be made.

This clause duplicates the disclosure warranty already given in Section 7(rr), adding a signed statement and a Servicing File retention duty. Whether the two clauses impose one obligation or two is left to construction.

For a second lien loan the clause warrants no uncured 'notice of default of a junior lien', which is backwards: the risk to a second lien holder is default under the senior lien, as Section 7(s)(3) and 7(m) confirm. The mistaken word changes what the representation covers.

'a higher-cost product designed for less creditworthy borrowers' and the exception for borrowers who 'did not qualify ... for a lower cost credit product' set no measurable test for steering. The clause also misspells 'debit-to-income' for debt-to-income.

'the principal determining factor' and 'a reasonable ability to make timely payments' are both unquantified standards applied to an underwriting methodology that is never identified. Whether a stated-income HELOC breaches this clause is squarely a matter of construction.

This clause warrants that 'no Revolving Credit Loan is subject to negative amortization', yet Section 7(w) requires every title policy to 'contain all applicable endorsements including a negative amortization endorsement, if applicable'. The instrument both denies and contemplates negative amortization.

The clause warrants the past and ongoing credit-reporting conduct of 'the Servicer', a term this Agreement never defines and which the recitals identify as GreenPoint, a non-party. Whose conduct EMC is warranting has to be worked out from the rest of the instrument.

This paragraph makes the Section 7 representations inure to 'the Purchaser, its successors and assigns' without qualification, while the recital on assignment says the representations and remedies pass to the Issuer only 'to the extent provided in the related Assignment Agreement'. Who holds the benefit of the warranties is left to be reconciled.

The proviso turns on 'a breach of the representation contained in clause CD) of this Section 7', a cross-reference that does not correspond to any lettered clause, so the second trigger for the prepayment-charge alternative remedy cannot be identified. The 90-day clock also runs from the earlier of the Seller's own 'discovery' or notice, leaving the trigger for the repurchase obligation contestable.

This repurchase protocol (notice, 90 days, cure/repurchase/substitute) overlaps with Section 5(d), which imposes its own separate Material Defect notice, 90-day cure and repurchase regime for missing or defective documents that the Section 7(gg) and 7(hhh) representations also cover. Which protocol governs a document breach is unresolved.

The clause makes a cause of action accrue only on the Seller's 'discovery' of a breach plus its failure to cure, repurchase or substitute, rather than on the making of the false representation. Whether that language postpones accrual — and the limitations period — is precisely what parties fight over.

Section 7 states that the representations are made 'as of the Closing Date', so a breach exists at closing, while this paragraph defers accrual until discovery and failure to cure. The two cannot easily be harmonised.

The clause warrants about 'the HELOC Seller's Information (as defined in Section 13(a) hereof)', but the table of contents makes Section 13 the indemnification section and Exhibit 3 separately carries the HELOC Seller's Information. The content of the warranted information depends on a cross-reference that must be checked against Section 13 and Exhibit 3.

The condition that the representations 'shall be true and correct as of the date or dates specified in all material respects' misplaces the materiality qualifier and leaves the 'date or dates specified' unidentified. What must be true, and when, is not clear from the sentence.

Section 10 sets out the conditions to the Purchaser's obligations, but Section 2(a) conditions the purchase and sale on 'the conditions set forth in Section 11 hereof' while Section 2(c) cites Section 10. Which section supplies the closing conditions is inconsistent across the instrument.

The clause promises 'all of the following closing documents' but no list follows in the instrument, and the only standard given is documents 'in such forms as are agreed upon and reasonably acceptable to the Purchaser'. What must be delivered as a condition to closing is therefore indeterminate.
